intro: Every four years, athletes march into a stadium behind their nation's flag. The Olympic Games began as a festival for Zeus at Olympia in ancient Greece. They came back in Athens in 1896 as a meeting of nations. Since then, countries have used the Games to show pride, to protest and sometimes to stay away.

At home, a different kind of paper changed rosters. In 1972 Congress passed Title IX, one sentence in an education law. It never names a sport. Yet it changed how many girls play on school teams, from about 294,000 in 1971–72 to more than three million.

In this unit you will read flags, oaths, votes, laws and court rulings. You will be able to explain who decides which nations and which students get a place, and you will be able to back up your answer with dates and documents.
bigQuestion: Who decides who gets a place on the team, for a nation at the Olympics or for a student at school?

words.d: the four-year period between one Olympic festival and the next
the body in each country that chooses and sends its Olympic team
a body that governs one sport across the world and writes its rules
refusing to take part in something as a protest
removing a member from an organization
South Africa's system of laws separating people by race

test.q: Where were the ancient Olympic Games held?
test.why: The ancient festival was held at the sanctuary of Zeus at Olympia.

test.q: When did the first modern Olympic Games open?
test.why: The first modern Games opened in Athens in April 1896.

test.q: Why did the 1904 Games leave Chicago?
choices: They joined the world's fair in St. Louis
test.why: The IOC moved the Games to St. Louis to be part of the Louisiana Purchase Exposition.

test.q: What first appeared at the Antwerp Games of 1920?
choices: The five-ring flag and the athletes' oath
test.why: The flag first flew and Victor Boin spoke the first oath in 1920.

test.q: Who sends a country's team to the Olympics?
test.why: Each National Olympic Committee chooses and sends its team.

test.q: Why did the United States lead a boycott in 1980?
test.why: The boycott protested the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan in December 1979.

test.q: What happened to South Africa's Olympic committee in 1970?
test.why: The IOC expelled it in 1970 because of apartheid in sport.

test.q: Which ritual began with the Berlin Games of 1936?
test.why: Carl Diem organized the first torch relay for Berlin in 1936.
President Nixon signed the Education Amendments of 1972 on June 23, 1972.

test.q: Which word does NOT appear in the Title IX sentence?
test.why: The sentence covers education programs but never names sport or athletics.

test.q: What did the Tower Amendment try to do in 1974?
choices: Exempt money-making sports from Title IX
test.why: Congress rejected Tower's plan to leave revenue sports out of Title IX.

test.q: Under the three-part test, how many parts must a school meet?
test.why: Meeting any one of the three parts is enough.

test.q: What did the Grove City decision of 1984 do?
choices: Limited Title IX to the program getting federal money
test.why: The Court limited Title IX to the specific program receiving federal money, until 1988.

test.q: Which pair shows the same kind of decision-maker?
choices: The IOC and a high school coach
An NOC and a state high school association
A world's fair and a court
A torch relay and a roster
test.why: Both are member bodies that decide who is sent or who gets a state series.

test.q: Which IHSA event came 85 years after the first boys wrestling champions?
choices: The first girls wrestling state finals
test.why: Boys wrestling champions date to 1937; the first girls finals were in 2022.

write.prompt: Who had more power to decide who could play: governments or sports bodies? Argue your answer using at least three dated records from this unit, such as the 1980 boycott vote, the IOC's 1970 expulsion of South Africa, Title IX (1972), the 1988 act or the IHSA's 2022 girls wrestling finals.
tips: Name each record and give its year.
Say who made each decision: a nation, the IOC, Congress, a court or the IHSA.
Compare one Olympic case with one school case.
Use unit words such as boycott, expulsion, regulations and sanctioned sport.
